summary: Addresses how to distribute routing policy data across multiple repositories and delegate authority over parts of it without weakening the authorization model from RFC 2725. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: Many libraries keep copies of the same map and let different librarians own different pages, safely.

questions: how is routing policy data replicated
what is the rpsl integrity attribute
what is a routing registry mirror
subtitle: How routing registries can copy each other's data and hand off parts of it, while every change is still checked for authorization.

tldr.problem: The Internet Routing Registry is used for things that need trustworthy data, and operators wanted to spread it over several less-trusted repositories without letting anyone sneak in unauthorized changes.
tldr.mechanism: Repositories flood signed, sequence-numbered transactions to their peers, who may repeat the authorization checks or rely on a trusted peer's signature. New RPSL objects and attributes (repository, delegated, integrity) describe who holds what.
tldr.outcome: A registry can be decentralized and mirrored, even down to a router acting as a minimal mirror, while the authorization model of RFC 2725 stays enforceable. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 2769 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2622 (RPSL) and RFC 2725 (routing policy system security).

sections.title: Replicating a Routing Registry
sections.content:
A routing registry is a repository of routing policy information, written in the RIPE database format and RPSL. The RFC says a registry must keep some degree of integrity to be of any use, and that the IRR is increasingly used for purposes with stronger requirements for integrity and security. This document proposes decentralizing the registry without compromising that integrity, even when the data is spread among less trusted repositories.

Two ways of protecting the data were considered. The first repeats authorization and authentication checks on each transaction as it is flooded, so each remote registry can choose to recheck. A party that trusts no repository can run its own mirror and recheck there. The second signs the objects themselves. The RFC argues this is flawed: to recheck an insertion you need the state of other objects, possibly in other repositories, so you would have to trace the change history back to a trusted point, and merely seeing that an object is signed does not show its addition was authorized. This RFC takes the first approach.

It distinguishes a repository, which does the initial checks for transactions on its local objects and floods them to adjacent repositories, from a mirror, which receives flooded transactions but is not authoritative for any objects. In the flooding topology they look identical.
sections.eli5: Instead of signing every page of the map, the libraries check each change when it is made. A library that trusts nobody can keep its own copy and do all the checking itself.

sections.title: Repositories and the ROOT Pointer
sections.content:
With several repositories, special repository objects announce that a repository exists and say how to use it. Each repository should also hold a repository object named ROOT, pointing to the root repository or a higher-level one, so a local query can still resolve hierarchically allocated objects across the full set of registries. The RFC says a root repository must be agreed upon, ideally holding only top-level delegations and pointers, and that it would be wise to allow only cryptographically strong transactions there.

A repository object lists its access methods and authentication types. query-address and submit-address are URLs, with rps-query or whois allowed as protocol identifiers for queries. response-auth-type and submit-auth-type list the authentication types it may use. repository-cert points to a public key certificate. heartbeat-interval and expire are durations written dddd hh:mm:ss.

If no heartbeat or new registrations arrive from a repository within its expire period, its objects are treated as non-authoritative and cannot be used for authorization. The expire value should be bigger than the heartbeat interval.
sections.eli5: There is a phone book that lists every library, how to ask each one questions, how to send it changes, and how often it promises to say hello. If a library goes quiet for too long, nobody trusts its pages until it checks in again.

sections.title: New RPSL Pieces: delegated and integrity
sections.content:
Beyond the repository object, the RFC adds two attributes. The delegated attribute may appear in object types that form a hierarchy (as-block, aut-num, inetnum and route). It says that further searches below that object must be made in the listed repositories. For example, an inetnum of 193.0.0.0 - 193.0.0.255 with delegated: RIPE passes storage of more specific overlapping objects to the RIPE repository. For authorization, only the mnt-by of the object in the repository being modified counts.

The integrity attribute records how far to trust an object. It is meant for a transition period, when some data predates a strong authorization model or some repositories do not check properly. If it is absent, the value is taken to be authorized. An object whose integrity is anything but authorized can be overwritten or deleted by any transaction that would have been a properly authorized addition without it. During the transition such data is only advisory.
sections.eli5: Delegating is like writing on a page, for anything smaller than this, ask the library across town. The integrity label is a sticker saying how much to trust a page, from a suspicious old one to one that was properly approved.

sections.title: Submitting a Transaction
sections.content:
A transaction can add, change or delete objects and is atomic: if any part fails, none of the changes take effect, so it can operate on only one database. Email submission of RFC-822 messages is still supported for backwards compatibility. The new encapsulation requires a user to append exactly one timestamp meta-object and one or more signature meta-objects, in that order. A repository must reject a transaction with no signature, and may reject one with no timestamp. The timestamp helps prevent replayed registrations, with the exact use left as a local matter.

As an example, the RFC shows a socket protocol in which the transaction sits between transaction-submit-begin and transaction-submit-end meta-objects carrying the same database name and identifier. The begin object can request a signed response and a confirmation type: none, legacy, normal or commit, optionally followed by verbose. Several transactions may be in flight at once and may finish out of order.

The reply is a transaction-confirm meta-object with a commit-status of succeeded, error or held. held is returned when a repository holding an object needed for authorization has expired.
sections.eli5: To send a change, you put your note in an envelope, stamp the time on it and sign it. The library can send back a receipt that says it worked, it failed, or it is waiting.

sections.title: Flooding, Polling, Heartbeats and Snapshots
sections.content:
Repositories keep TCP connections to their peers. After committing a submitted transaction, the originating repository assigns it a sequence number, signs and encapsulates it, and sends a copy to each peer. The first transaction gets sequence number 1, successive ones get successive numbers, and sequence numbers must come from a range at least as large as 64 bit unsigned integers. The redistributed text is the transaction plus a transaction-label (database, sequence, timestamp, optional integrity), optional auth-dependency objects naming other repositories whose objects were used for authorization, and a final repository-signature. It is wrapped by a transaction-begin object giving its length and a transfer-method of plain or gzip.

A receiver decodes the text, silently discards a transaction it has already seen, and verifies the originator's signature. It must hold a transaction if earlier ones from the same repository are missing. Unless a trusted repository's signature lets it skip ahead, it checks syntax and then authorizes and authenticates the transaction, holding it if needed objects are missing. A failed transaction is still redistributed so there is no gap in the sequence.

Three other mechanisms support this. A transaction-request asks a peer for a range of transactions, which is how mirrors poll or catch up. Each repository that has originated at least one transaction must send periodic heartbeat meta-objects, at an interval less than 1 day, so others can tell it is alive. An optional commit protocol uses commit-request and commit-response to confirm that another repository has accepted a transaction. Finally, a database snapshot is a set of files (X.db, optional per-class files and X.transaction-label) transferred out of band, for initializing a new repository or disaster recovery.
sections.eli5: Each library numbers its changes 1, 2, 3 and passes them to its neighbors, who pass them on. A short regular hello shows a library is still there, and a neighbor that missed some changes can ask for the ones in between.

sections.title: Authentication, Authorization and Trust
sections.content:
The RFC separates the two ideas. Authentication determines who is attempting a change, and authorization determines whether that identity may perform the operation. Authorization depends on related objects: their mnt-by, mnt-routes or mnt-lower attributes point to maintainer objects whose auth attributes hold the method and, generally, a public key. No encryption capability is specified, because of import, export and use restrictions around the world, and transactions must not be encrypted.

The RPSL objects themselves are not signed. The whole transaction body is. Signatures should cover the original content and not other signatures, so they can be checked in any order, and a transaction must remain intact even if a repository does not use one of the submitter's authentication methods. If the signature of a trusted repository is found, no further authorization or authentication is needed. Appendix B describes the spectrum: if all repositories trust each other, nobody repeats checks, and if none do, every repository checks every transaction. In practice a repository trusts a subset, and trust need not be mutual.

Repositories are told to err on the side of denying a transaction, since accepting a bad one requires later removing its effects. A failed authorization check at a receiver stalls further advancement until the originating repository fixes the problem.
sections.eli5: A signed note proves who wrote it, and the map owner's rules say whether that person may change that page. If you trust a neighbor who already checked, you do not have to check again.

sections.title: Deployment, Router Mirrors and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a staged transition: first change the existing near real time mirroring format to follow this document, then add the commit protocol and confirmations, then add remote rechecking of authorization (until then all repositories must be trusted), and finally allow further decentralization.

It also sketches a router acting as a minimal mirror. Such a router needs no code for rechecking authorization, submission, queries or commits, must be adjacent only to trusted mirrors (generally run by the same organization), checks only the adjacent mirror's signature, and may discard object types not needed for route filters. The RFC estimates about 100 transactions per day and notes a router could write to flash only every few days and then request a transaction range after a crash.

On privacy, person and role objects contain contact information and should not be redistributed by default. Fields that need an email address must also accept a NIC-handle. Objects cannot be redistributed with attributes removed, because that would invalidate the signature, and a transaction should not mix redistributable and non-redistributable objects. The closing security section simply says the protocol lets all registries follow the model of RFC 2725 and lets deviations be noticed by other registries or mirrors.
sections.eli5: Even a small box like a router could keep a copy of the map if it only listens to a neighbor it trusts. Private phone numbers stay with the library that owns them.

items.label: Legacy
items.desc: Existed before an adequate authorization model; highly suspect.

items.label: No authorization
items.desc: Added during the transition, but authorization depended on objects that were not authorized.

items.label: Authorization failed
items.desc: The authoritative repository is not checking authorization; it would have failed if it did.

items.label: Authorized
items.desc: Authorization checks passed. This is the default when the attribute is absent.
